entries.content:
How Bright Machines streams factory changes out of air-gapped plants with Debezium, Apache Iceberg and Unity Catalog, so customers see live, governed dashboards with no inbound access to the plant

by Jitesh Soni, Anup Chatterjee, Bryan Whittington, Mark Loesel, Mauricio Caro, Caitlin Gordon and Rachel Musiker

  • Live factory data from an air-gapped plant: Bright Machines captures PostgreSQL changes at the edge with Debezium and writes them as Apache Iceberg. The data goes out over one auditable outbound path, and Databricks reads it in place through Unity Catalog federation with AWS Glue.
  • One governed platform replaces a nine-service pipeline: The old pipeline broke when schemas changed, failures went unnoticed and it had no real access controls. Now one Unity Catalog-governed platform serves role-based AI/BI Dashboards and zero-copy shares.
  • Results: Data can be queried in Databricks 1–2 minutes after it's written on the line, and dashboards refresh every 10 minutes. A heartbeat check catches a broken pipeline in under 30 minutes instead of days, and the first customer dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Bright Machines gives customers live, governed dashboards of their factory data without opening any inbound access to its air-gapped plants. It captures PostgreSQL changes at the factory edge with Debezium, writes them as Apache Iceberg, sends them out over a single auditable outbound path, and reads them in place in Databricks through Unity Catalog federation. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

  • Problem: customers wanted factory data, and the only way to share it was reports rerun on-prem and sent over by email.
  • Solution: Debezium change data capture, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue, Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, AI/BI Dashboards and OpenSharing.
  • Result: nine loosely coupled services replaced by one governed platform plus one edge path, with zero inbound ports to the plant.
  • Freshness: a row committed on the line is queryable in Databricks in one to two minutes, and dashboards refresh every ten minutes.
  • Monitoring: a heartbeat check detects a broken pipeline in under thirty minutes, down from days.

Every time a customer visited one of our factory floors, the same thing happened. They would stand in front of the assembly dashboard, watch the line run, and ask for a copy of the data: yield by station, cycle time trends, downtime by cause, the genealogy of a batch.

We had all of it. We had built those dashboards for our own operations team, and they ran on the floor against the line databases. A customer could not access any of it directly over the internet. The plant is air gapped by design: no inbound access, one tightly controlled route out, and role-based access rules that restricted access in.

Each new report required data engineering to reshape data through multiple ETL jobs, costing hours to days of engineering time.

Bright Machines builds software-defined, automation-first production lines that run inside our customers' plants. Those plants are locked down by design: no inbound access, minimal outbound, and zero tolerance for risk. Each line runs a stack of on-premises services (our in-house MES, integrations with customer's MES, operator screens, robot workflow orchestrators, and the assembly dashboards) that all persist to PostgreSQL on the factory's on-prem cluster. The software team that runs this is a lean team and manages the data pipelines end to end as well as the data applications software stack. The data drives various KPI dashboards, finance reporting, operations, quality, vendor component quality, NCR tracking, genealogy, OEE and the downtime and cycle-time analysis behind every shift.

On our first attempt to solve this problem, we rebuilt a cloud copy of each factory database from application events, across nine loosely coupled services. On the factory floor the picture was fine. Everything off the floor was the problem with this complex architecture and pipeline.

The nine services were a message broker, a custom shoveler, a queue, object storage, few serverless functions, a cloud relational database, a scheduler, an ETL pipeline, and a popular open source BI tool with very basic RBAC support.

The pipeline failed for these reasons:

  • Schema Evolution. Schemas changed often, and the pipeline silently dropped changed data unless the ETL jobs were updated every time an on-prem dashboard or schema changed.
  • Missing monitoring. The pipeline had failures and the dead-letter queues were a pain to monitor, so missed or duplicated events went unnoticed.
  • Data validation. Once data landed in a bucket, nobody could say with confidence if it was accurate and from the right source.
  • Data Governance. Having proper governance and role based access controls over views and data that we shared.

Fixing all the above features needed rearchitecting from the ground up.

In addition to the above reasons these constraints also shaped the new design:

Security Model. No inbound connectivity to the plant, and all access auditable.

Governance we could demonstrate. A customer would see exactly what their role allowed on the floor, and we had to be able to prove the appropriate limits were in place.

Freshness in minutes. A dashboard view that is on prem would be visible in a few minutes over the internet with the same data.

The new architecture:

Bright Machines chose edge change data capture with Unity Catalog federation because it was the only option where no compute outside a customer's and/or Bright Machines' own accounts touched factory data before governance is applied.

Our criteria, in order: access control that matched what was already enforced on the floor, one outbound auditable path we could explain to any security team, minute-level freshness, and open formats at the edge.

We worked through the options with our Databricks solutions architect before writing any code. The two obvious ones were Lakeflow Connect ingesting directly from PostgreSQL, and a Postgres export picked up by Auto Loader. Both would have been faster to stand up. Our threat model followed the rule that data can be pushed out, but nothing outside can reach in. A pull-based ingestion pattern needs a network path from the cloud to the factory database, and running ingestion in an environment outside the accounts where the data resided. So the question became: how do we get the same governed result while keeping every piece that touches raw factory data inside environments we own?

The answer was to flip the direction. Capture changes at the edge, land them in an open format, push them out over one auditable path, and let Databricks read them in place.

We proved it on a replicated line, similar to that of a production site, with two engineers over about six weeks. The bar had two parts. First, a row committed on the line had to be queryable in under five minutes with no inbound port opened. Second, a customer principal had to see exactly the tables and dashboards their role allowed, and nothing else.

The deciding factor was that Databricks already enforced the security model that aligned with ours: Unity Catalog for who can see what, and OpenSharing to publish governed tables without copies. Going in, we worried that governance on federated tables would not be strict enough for the audit. It was strict, and the strictness that tripped us up during cutover is the same strictness we rely on now.

Data leaves the factory in five steps, over a single outbound path, and Databricks reads it in place without a copy job. Operators keep the on-prem assembly dashboard, because they need real time. Databricks cloud serves customers and internal teams.

Capture at the edge with Debezium. Debezium Server tails the PostgreSQL replication slot and writes an append-only Apache Iceberg change log to a local object store. If the WAN drops, the backlog becomes objects on the floor, not write-ahead log piling up on the production database.

Send it out over one path. A single edge component copies each object to a bucket in the site's cloud account. It is the only outbound data path from the plant, and its credentials can write to that one bucket and nothing else. Cross-account replication carries the objects to the analytics account.

Federate it into Unity Catalog. The Iceberg tables are registered in AWS Glue, and Unity Catalog federates Glue as a read-only catalog. That makes over a hundred tables across factory PostgreSQL databases queryable in Databricks with no copy.

Model it in Databricks SQL. Bronze views collapse the change log to the current state. A Lakeflow Job rebuilds silver models every ten minutes, all in SQL and deployed from Git with Databricks Asset Bundles.

Serve it with dashboards and OpenSharing. Multiple AI/BI Dashboards read processed data from the silver layer with role-based permissions. This allowed external customers and internal teams to all see the same numbers. OpenSharing allows the same copy of data to be shared securely to our customers.

Registering the tables in AWS Glue lets Bright Machines control exactly when each table moves forward. A change log on object storage is a stream of new metadata files. A small function advances each table's pointer in Glue only when a new metadata file has fully replicated, and only forward. Glue holds the pointer, Unity Catalog holds the permissions, and Databricks only ever reads the version we have validated.

Use a heartbeat. When a line stops for a shift change, no new rows arrive, and that looks exactly like a broken pipeline. Row counts cannot tell the two extremes apart.

Debezium updates a one-row heartbeat table in each source database every five minutes, whether or not the line is running. That update travels the same path as production data. The first task of the Lakeflow Job checks the heartbeat, and if any is more than thirty minutes old, the task fails and the whole job goes red. Dashboards keep showing the last good data instead of presenting stale data as current.

We phased it in four steps: 1.) a pilot on a PoC line, 2.) going live with the highest-value production line, 3.) a parallel run against the old snapshot path to check row for row parity, and 4.) a hard cutover of the dashboards for customers.

What surprised us. Scale showed up in the wrong dimension. We moved a few 100 gigabytes a day, but as hundreds of thousands of small objects, so every design decision ended up being about object rate rather than dictated by bytes.

What we would do differently. Build the reconciliation pass on day one. A sync driven by create events never goes back for an object it missed, and nothing downstream notices until a query touches it.

The focus of those customer visits changed. Nobody asks for a copy of the dashboard any more, because they already have it, under the roles available to them. A customer analyst opens the Quality dashboard from their desk and sees the same numbers the line lead sees on the floor, within about ten minutes of them happening. We never run a report. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Five lessons for anyone sharing data from a locked-down site:

  • Start from the security model you already have. Our data governance requirements defined the roles and restrictions. We picked the platform that enforced exactly those, rather than approximating them.
  • Design the one path out first, and buffer behind it. A single auditable egress makes every later conversation with a security team manageable. Buffering at the edge means a WAN blip never becomes a production database incident.
  • Keep control of when a table moves forward. A catalog hop you own, with a guard on the pointer, means the lakehouse only ever sees a version you have validated.
  • Build the data once and let permissions do the rest. Maintaining a customer version and an operations version of every report was what ate the hours.
  • Assert freshness on a heartbeat, not on row counts. No new rows means the line is idle. No new heartbeat means the pipeline is broken.

Now that the data is governed and accessible, the next step is to make this more accessible to AI features through natural language analytics with Genie, custom AI agents for operations, and predictive analytics that turn factory data into forward-looking decisions.

Having custom AI agents for operational analytics and investigations. The people who work on those lines - operators, quality engineers, maintenance techs have domain expertise but aren't SQL users. Custom AI agents (via Databricks Apps or Agent Bricks) could let a line lead ask "Why did station 4 have higher downtime this shift?" Bright Machines provided knowledge docs along with operational data could get an answer grounded in the same governed silver data. This is the "improve the bottom line" play — reducing the time from question to action on the factory floor.

Q: Can Databricks be used with an air-gapped factory?

Yes. Bright Machines keeps zero inbound ports open to the plant for data. Changes are captured inside the factory and pushed out over one auditable outbound path, and Databricks reads the resulting Apache Iceberg tables in place through Unity Catalog federation.

Q: How fresh is the factory data in Databricks?

A row committed on the line is queryable in Databricks in one to two minutes at steady state. Silver models and dashboards refresh every ten minutes. Operators who need real time views keep using the on-prem assembly dashboards.

Q: How do customers access the data?

In two ways: AI/BI Dashboards with role-based permissions integrated with Bright Machine’s SSO Federation, and additional capability to provide OpenSharing access, which publishes zero copy governed silver tables to customers with Databricks accounts.

Q: What replaced the old nine-service pipeline?

One governed platform, Databricks, plus a single edge path made up of Debezium, a local object store and one sync component. Bronze views, silver models, the job, the dashboards and the shares are all deployed from one Databricks Asset Bundle.

Q: This design was specifically built on AWS, does the design work on Azure or Google Cloud?

The cloud-specific parts are the edge sync target, the cross-account replication and the catalog hop. Everything on the Databricks side is the same on any cloud, so moving it is a change to a few resources rather than a rebuild.

Q: How long did it take?

The proof of concept took about six weeks with two engineers. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Want to share governed data from locked-down sites without opening inbound access? Learn how Unity Catalog federates Apache Iceberg tables from AWS Glue, or talk to your Databricks account team about your architecture.

entries.content:
How to spot adversaries who sign in with stolen credentials, using Databricks verbose audit logs and Genie

by Solomon Boyd, Alexis Merritt, Arun Pamulapati, Sam Pezzino and David Veuve

  • Learn how adversaries use stolen credentials to sign in to Databricks and blend in with normal user activity.
  • Explore how system tables and the Detection App's Genie agent spot behavior shifts across six stages of an attack.
  • Get ready-to-run detection and response queries, plus the ingress and least-privilege controls that limit what a stolen credential can reach.

At Databricks, we know your data is your most valuable asset. Databricks has worked with thousands of customers to securely deploy the Databricks Data + AI Platform with the appropriate features to meet their security, privacy, and regulatory requirements.

The modern cyberattack does not always begin with a shattered perimeter; it begins with a valid login. Once an adversary acquires a leaked session cookie, personal access token (PAT), or service-principal credential, the initial breach is already complete. From that moment on, their entire goal is to blend in and operate under the guise of your compromised user or service.

But having a key doesn't mean you know the building. Imagine an intruder swiping a badge to enter a secure office. They may have cleared the revolving doors, but they still have to navigate the security guard, guess which floors they have access to, and figure out where the vault is. Because an attacker lacks the deep, localized context of your actual employees, their behavior will eventually betray them. Spotting those irregularities is how you catch them.

In this post, we walk through how a credential-driven attack unfolds on the Databricks platform, how to detect the shift in an identity’s behavior using Databricks verbose audit logs and Genie, how to respond once you confirm a compromise, and which controls limit what a stolen credential can do in the first place.

When establishing access via legitimate credentials, adversaries, like security practitioners, also understand their access may get revoked at any point when they deviate too greatly from the identity’s expected behavior. Adversaries rely on non-linear attack sequencing, such as validating one set of credentials to map your environment, then retrieving another set of credentials to return through a new identity or workspace that doesn’t have reconnaissance activity associated with it. Additionally, adversaries may gather information without establishing persistence or establish their way back into your Databricks platform before wrapping up their objectives.

Consider a data engineer whose personal access token is copied from a misconfigured continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) log. Within minutes, the token is used from a new IP to list secret scopes, catalogs, and repos across the workspace, something this engineer has never done. A secret holding a service-principal credential is read. An hour later, that service principal, not the engineer, creates a function, adds itself to an admin group, and exports a handful of init scripts. Each of these events could pass as routine platform use, but taken together they show one intrusion moving through the attack chain.

At Databricks, we expect non-linear event sequencing in relation to credential-driven attacks and use this model to connect individual events into one investigation rather than treating them as unrelated events.

When adversaries leverage compromised credentials in a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) environment, such as Databricks, their activity can be grouped into six stages, although they rarely move through them in a straight line. Each stage below describes what the adversary is trying to do and what to look for in Databricks audit logging tables. Treat this guidance as a starting point and tune it to your environment's normal automation.

Note: Events are written as 

service_name.action_name
, for example 
secrets.getSecret
.

The login itself rarely looks unusual. Because the credential is real, authentication succeeds as it would for the legitimate owner. However, what the identity does in the minutes after signing in often looks very different from its normal activity, and that change is what responders can detect. In the data engineer example, the stolen token authenticates successfully, and the only difference at login is a source IP the engineer has never used. The activity that follows is what stands out.

Adversary goal: Access the workspace with valid credentials, whether a stolen browser session, a replayed PAT, or a service-principal credential, and blend into activity the controls are designed to allow.

What to look for:

  • Use the authentication event as the starting point for your timeline. A login alone is rarely enough to alert on, but its 
    user_identity
    , 
    source_ip_address, user_agent
    , 
    sessionId
    , 
    request_id
    , and 
    workspace_id
    let you follow what the credential does next.
  • Flag 
    accounts.tokenLogin
    events that arrive in a short burst from an unfamiliar client and are followed by use of the same token from a different source IP. This pattern can indicate that someone is testing a stolen token, and 
    requestParams.tokenId
    lets you tie those events to the same token.
  • Flag service-principal OAuth tokens that are minted from the expected network with an unexpected user agent, especially when activity from a new source IP follows within a minute.

Next, the adversary needs to learn what the credential can reach before the access is revoked. As a result, a compromised identity can shift from its ordinary activity to listing data, secrets, code, and network controls within seconds. This reconnaissance usually spans several services at once and moves faster than a person navigating the UI. In our scenario, this stage is the burst of calls listing secret scopes, catalogs, and repos within minutes of the token being used, which is activity the engineer has never performed before.

Adversary goal: Build a map of accessible data, credentials, repositories, and guardrails to plan a path deeper into the environment before access is revoked.

  • Look for a single identity making rapid list calls across the workspace and account planes, such as 
    secrets.listScopes
    / 
    listSecrets
    , 
    unityCatalog.listMetastores
    / 
    listCatalogs
    / 
    listSchemas
    / 
    listExternalLocations
    / 
    listStorageCredentials
    , 
    repos.listRepos
    , and account-level 
    accountsManager.listWorkspaceConfigurations
    / 
    listNetworkConfigurations
    / 
    listStorageConfigurations
    . For example, five or more distinct discovery APIs called within one minute is unlikely to be a person navigating the platform.
  • Compare activity to the identity's baseline. The first secret enumeration ever made by an established identity, or a SQL session that shifts from business queries to 
    SHOW TABLES
    against access-control and configuration schemas, is more meaningful than a high volume of calls. When verbose audit logging is enabled, 
    commandSubmit
    preserves the query in 
    commandText
    .
  • Include failed requests in your search. Investigate an identity's first 
    IpAccessDenied
    , especially when it follows 
    accounts.oidcTokenAuthorization
    or repeats across workspaces. In that case, authorization succeeded but the request came from a blocked network, which is often the earliest record of a credential being replayed from an untrusted location.

Harvesting credentials usually takes several steps. The adversary lists secret scopes, lists the secrets in them, and then reads the ones that look useful. The value they retrieve allows them to return as a different, often more privileged, identity. For this reason, every secret read by a suspect identity is worth following up on. In the data engineer example, the adversary reads a secret that holds a service-principal credential. From that point on, the investigation has to follow two identities: the engineer and the service principal.

Adversary goal: Retrieve a token, API key, or service-principal secret that upgrades the initial foothold into environment-wide access under a new identity.

  • Alert on the progression of calls. 
    secrets.listScopes
    on its own is common and generates noise. However, 
    listScopes
    followed by 
    listSecrets
    and then 
    getSecret
    , repeated across multiple scopes in quick succession, indicates harvesting. 
    listSecrets
    records the scope, and 
    getSecret
    records both the scope and the key.
  • Correlate denied reads with later successful ones. A denied 
    getSecret
    on a tightly controlled scope, followed by a successful read of the same or a related key in a less restricted scope, suggests the identity is looking for a copy it can access.
  • Monitor compute-side access in addition to the secrets API. When verbose audit logging is enabled, notebook 
    submitCommand
    and Databricks SQL 
    commandSubmit
    events can show code calling secret utilities or running 
    read_files()
    against paths that contain credentials. Keep in mind that the submitted text shows what ran, but it does not confirm that a value was returned.
  • Connect each secret read to what happens next, such as a new 
    accounts.tokenLogin
    , first-seen service-principal activity, a changed IP or user agent, or 
    generateTemporaryTableCredential
    / 
    generateTemporaryVolumeCredential
    calls. During response, rotate every credential the identity could have reached, and check where each one was used in addition to where it was stored.

Once access is established, adversaries look for a way to run their own code. On Databricks, this typically happens through user-defined functions (UDFs) and jobs. A function can wrap a payload in ordinary-looking code that can be called repeatedly, and a job can run that code on a schedule across different compute. As such, the key question for detection is whether an identity has started performing actions it has not performed before. Returning to the data engineer, an hour after the secret is read, the service principal creates a function. Because the service principal, rather than the engineer, performs this action, a search scoped only to the engineer's activity would miss it.

Adversary goal: Establish a reliable, reusable way to execute payloads, with a fallback when one compute route is blocked.

  • Prioritize createFunction events from an identity, IP, or catalog with no history of creating functions, especially when several appear in a short period. Where function definitions are available, flag code that executes processes, evaluates code dynamically, accesses instance metadata, opens outbound network connections, or writes to cloud storage. Also trace references between functions, because a harmless-looking wrapper can call a higher-risk UDF. Note that 
    function_info
    in 
    system.access.audit
    is masked except for account admins and 
    databricks_pii_access
    , so pair audit data with function inventories.
  • Track the Jobs path by identity, IP, and job or run ID. A typical sequence is 
    importNotebook
    , then 
    changeJobAcl
    , 
    Jobs create
    , 
    runNow
    , and 
    getRunOutput
    . These events rarely preserve the notebook body, so retain notebook versions and job configurations alongside them. Repeated import-and-run activity from one source is a stronger signal than either action alone.
  • Look for an identity that switches compute after a failure. For example, a failed cluster creation or 
    submitRun
    followed shortly by 
    startWarehouse
    , or by a new job on different compute, may indicate an adversary working around a blocked path. The response codes and the short gap between events are what separate this sequence from routine errors. Serverless compute is a common fallback.

With a way to run code, adversaries next try to make sure they can return after the original credential is revoked. Common persistence methods include access grants, newly created tokens, group and workspace membership changes, and control-plane edits. The most useful signal is a sensitive change made by an unfamiliar identity or execution context. For example, a permission change made from inside a job deserves more scrutiny than the same change made by an administrator in the console. Next in the scenario, the service principal adds itself to an admin group. Even if the engineer's token is revoked, that group membership keeps the adversary's access in place.

Adversary goal: Create durable, independent access paths that survive revocation of the compromised credential.

  • Alert on permission and identity grants from unexpected contexts, such as 
    putAcl
    on a secret scope, 
    updatePermissionAssignment
    , 
    addPrincipalToGroup
    , or 
    setAdmin
    . Pay particular attention when a service principal grants another identity access, or when multiple assignments occur in a short period.
  • Treat attempts to change security controls as high severity, even when they fail. This includes 
    setSetting
    / 
    deleteSetting
    , IP access-list edits, and 
    createPrivateAccessSettings
    . Review the requested change, the response, and the source before concluding whether a control was actually bypassed. Also review SCIM group changes from anything other than the expected IdP.
  • Flag 
    generateDbToken
    calls from an unfamiliar source or during a job run. Each resulting token is a separate credential that will need to be revoked.
  • Watch for workloads that continue on their own. Correlate control-plane events with 
    run_by
    , 
    run_as
    , and the expected run window. If a job keeps modifying groups, permissions, or settings after the adversary's interactive activity stops, it may be maintaining access by itself. Preserve the job definition and artifacts before terminating it.

Data collection can be as small as a few targeted exports, and cleanup can involve more than deleting files. Watch for targeted exports, temporary-credential requests, removal of short-lived tooling, and obfuscated commands that make the activity harder to reconstruct. Any one of these events can look routine, so the sequence around them matters more than the individual export or delete. Finally, the service principal from our scenario exports a handful of init scripts. On its own, that is a small export. However, because it follows a secret read and a new function from the same service principal, it should be investigated as part of the same intrusion.

Adversary goal: Take the data that matters and erase the most obvious tooling while leaving quieter access in place.

  • Look at the context of each export rather than the number of exports. 
    workspaceExport
    records the path, the format, and whether it was a direct download. Prioritize exports by unfamiliar identities, to unusual paths or in unusual formats, from previously unseen networks, or that follow secret access or new execution. A small, targeted export of init scripts can leak more than a bulk 
    SOURCE
    dump.
  • Keep records of short-lived objects. A 
    createFunction
    followed by 
    deleteFunction
    for the same function in one session, or a repeated create, delete, and recreate cycle, may indicate an attempt to remove evidence. Preserve the definitions and timing before reverting anything. Objects that survive are often given more plausible names than the ones that were deleted.
  • Connect temporary-credential and data-read bursts (
    generateTemporaryTableCredential
    , 
    generateTemporaryVolumeCredential
    , Delta Sharing, cloud-storage reads) to earlier reconnaissance. Encoded or scripted commands are too common to alert on by themselves, so correlate them with an unfamiliar user agent, automation-like timing, secret access, or new functions.

Using the credential-driven attack chain as a guide, you can direct Genie to work through the attack stages without writing every query from scratch. Every detection in this post runs on telemetry you already have. Databricks writes control-plane activity to the 

system.access.audit
system table.

To get started, install the Detection App, which adds a Genie agent for Databricks’ audit logging. You can work it from Genie One in two ways:

  • Ask in your own words, like "Which notebooks did user@example.com export yesterday?" Genie writes and runs the SQL for you.
  • Use the built-in detections. The Detection App Genie agent includes more than 30 detections, ranging from token misuse to admin grants. Ask "Who created personal access tokens last week?" and Genie runs the matching detection instead of writing new SQL. Give it a goal, like "Were we compromised in the last 90 days?", and it works through the detections one at a time.

Keep two limits in mind. First, an empty result doesn't mean nothing happened. The event may be outside your time window, or verbose audit logging may be disabled. Second, audit logs record that something changed and who changed it, but often not the old or new values.

Once a hunt surfaces an identity that doesn't fit its normal pattern, the focus shifts to what access the adversary still has. Because credential-driven attacks are non-linear, the first access you find is rarely the only access. In the data engineer example, revoking the engineer's token would leave the service principal's credential, its admin group membership, and the function it created in place. A complete response removes the original credential as well as every path the adversary created afterward, including grants, tokens, functions, and jobs that keep running after the user is disabled.

For a suspected workspace compromise, responders should:

  • Disable the identity. Deactivate the user at the account level, which blocks every workspace. There's no API to end a user's browser sessions, but deactivation blocks them. For a service principal, delete its OAuth secrets and deactivate it with the account SCIM API. OAuth tokens that the service principal already has stay valid for up to an hour.
  • Revoke their personal access tokens. Deactivating a user doesn't delete their tokens, and the tokens work again if the user is reactivated. Use the Token Management API or the token report in the account console.
  • Save what you need, then stop the compute. Export job definitions and notebook versions first. Then cancel job runs, terminate clusters, and stop SQL warehouses. On serverless, cancel the run or statement. Deactivating a user doesn't stop compute that's already running.
  • Rotate every secret the actor read. Change it at the source, then update the stored value. Rotate the credential the adversary used to get in, too.
  • Undo actor-created persistence. Remove secret scope ACLs, workspace assignments, and group memberships. Drop the functions and revoke the grants. Restore your context-based ingress policies (and IP access lists, if you still use them) from your own records.
  • Check code the identity could change outside Databricks, like init scripts and ETL code in cloud storage.
  • Confirm it stopped. Run a search on activity by the actor. If verbose audit logging was off, turn it on. Command text is only logged while it's on.

To return to the office building: context-based ingress decides who gets through the revolving doors, and least privilege decides which floors their badge can open. Early detection buys response time, but preventive controls limit what a stolen credential can do. The controls below are grouped by what they take away from the adversary, in roughly the order they break their attack chain.

The strongest preventive control against credential reuse is context-based ingress control. It evaluates who is making a request, where it comes from, and what it is for, instead of relying on a single network perimeter. This is especially useful as more organizations move away from VPNs. Even without a corporate network to anchor on, you can limit a stolen token to the contexts its owner actually uses. For example, you can restrict a privileged service principal to API requests from trusted networks while applying a different policy to human users.

  • Apply policies to both workspace and account requests. Workspace policies don't cover the account console or account-level APIs.
  • Start in dry-run mode. Review denials and dry-run violations in 
    system.access.inbound_network
    , protect privileged service principals first, and enforce after you've accounted for legitimate automation and partner integrations.
  • Test serverless and private-connectivity workflows before broad enforcement, because they follow separate policy rules. Document any exceptions and monitor their use.
  • Treat IP access lists as an additional layer. Where both apply, a request must pass both. Configure workspace and account-console lists if you still use them.
  • Set expiration and rotation requirements for service-principal credentials, integration credentials, and personal access tokens, and retire credentials that are no longer used. Dormant credentials are particularly attractive to adversaries because a compromise can go unnoticed for months.
  • Enforce least privilege on secret scopes. Avoid storing copies of powerful credentials in scopes with different ACLs, and review who can list scope contents as well as who can retrieve values.
  • Restrict high-impact operations. Limit UDF creation, secret-scope ACL changes, workspace permission changes, job administration, and ingress policy changes to approved identities and controlled automation.
  • Separate administrative paths from compute paths. Ordinary job runtimes should not be able to modify account and network controls, and any attempt to do so should generate an alert.
  • Protect cloud execution environments. Use hardened metadata-service configurations where applicable and restrict egress from compute so workloads cannot freely reach credential endpoints or unapproved destinations.
  • Restrict which identities can manage account identities, assign workspace access, and create jobs.
  • Preserve investigation-ready telemetry for potential security compromises.
  • Retain audit logs, notebook and job version history, UDF definitions and dependencies, permission-change history, cloud-storage write events, and context-based-ingress denial logs long enough to reconstruct a campaign.

Remember, a stolen credential’s blast radius is only as damaging as the privileges assigned to it. Reduce that exposure and be able to hunt for anomalous activity by taking these steps:

  • Review the Databricks security best practices to harden your workspaces and account.
  • Turn on verbose audit logging and set up context-based ingress control so both planes are covered.
  • Deploy the Detection App to start your hunts and ask Genie your first question: "Were we compromised in the last 90 days?"

How a Lead Solutions Architect scales AI solutions in financial services

  • The Databricks Field Engineering team helps our customers build and scale AI solutions.
  • Enterprises are replacing slow, legacy data stacks to eliminate data silos and overcome complex risk modeling, governance, and compliance workflows.
  • Learn what a typical week looks like for a lead solutions architect.

Q: What does a typical week look like for a Lead Solutions Architect, and how would you describe the pace?

A: Senior field engineers balance building tech with coaching colleagues. On any given day, I might code an app to solve a customer challenge, scale that application for another account, or partner directly with executive management on a business case. I switch fluidly between player and coach. Platforms like Lakebase high-scale OLTP continuously expand our addressable scope, but the core mission remains unchanged: delivering measurable impact to customers as a connected team.

Q: You spent two decades on the customer side in financial services before joining Databricks. What drove the switch, and what keeps you energized?

A: I’ve known Databricks since its founding and discussed investments with chairman Ion Stoica back in 2014. But when I used the product hands-on, I laughed out loud; tasks that took days or weeks on traditional stacks ran in seconds or minutes. I knew I had to join to help solve the world’s toughest data problems at scale. In just 12 months, tools like Agentbricks, Lakebase, and AI Apps transformed us from optimizing existing FSI processes to completely redesigning them on Databricks.

Q: How do cultural principles like "Customer Obsessed" and "Truth-Seeking" come to life in your work?

A: Meeting customers where they are requires deep preparation, analyzing annual reports, analyst guidance, and industry news to surface key risks and opportunities.

Recently, at a top European asset manager, a boardroom AI discussion started with "What is a token?" Within 20 minutes on Databricks, I demonstrated how to analyze Private Credit risks, set warning indicators, and use Document Intelligence AI to identify hidden contagion risks across debt covenants. We completely reshaped the board's perspective on what’s possible with real-time risk modeling and portfolio hedging.

Q4: What is internal collaboration like across Field Engineering and regional teams?

A: Moving from traditional corporate hierarchies to Databricks’ open, transparent culture was a shift. In my first month, I aligned on EMEA priorities with our GTM FSI leader, and by month two, we were executing. The FSI SME groups collaborate instantly across time zones; I even watched our APAC colleagues present one of our custom demos to a customer in Tokyo in Japanese.

Q: What makes Databricks’ technical approach to Financial Services unique?

A: Our Apache Spark™ heritage paired with Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway are our superpowers. They enable customers to execute complex AI/ML workloads with full governance and control, critical for risk management across credit, market, underwriting, and compliance.

  • Banking: Banks transition from annual KYC checks to real-time, "Perpetual KYC."
  • Insurance: Insurers deploy Agentic AI in claims processing to cut costs while boosting customer NPS.
  • Capital Markets: Global trading institutions execute liquidity calculations every 5 minutes (down from twice daily) during peak geopolitical volatility.

Q: What do high-profile strategic engagements signal to candidates about their potential impact here?

A: Databricks acts as a trusted strategic advisor to world leaders in finance. Our customers process trillions of dollars daily and insure risk equal to national GDPs. When executive teams choose Databricks, they rely on us to power core operations and guide multi-billion-dollar strategic changes that impact millions of people.

Q: How does internal community participation drive success in FSI?

A: FSI thrives on community. Our Slack channels serve as a real-time pulse, where global teams solve niche, complex customer challenges daily. Openness and radical transparency allow anyone to reach out and collaborate with confidence.

Q: How should early-career candidates balance building domain expertise alongside technical skills?

A: Domain knowledge makes you relevant to customers. You gain deep domain expertise by steering major business transformations, which requires both solid tech fundamentals and active listening. Always align technical projects to overarching business goals. Stay curious, read widely (like the FT Book of the Year list), and seek to understand human incentives, because strategic business decisions are always made by people.

Q9: What traits separate Solutions Architects who truly excel?

A: Success isn't one-size-fits-all. Some excel as deep technical specialists in specific products like Unity Gateway or Genie; others become trusted vertical experts. The common denominator is trust; if your customers, partners, and peers trust you, you will succeed.

Ready to build alongside a team that is solving the world’s toughest problems? We’re hiring. See our open roles.

entries.content:
New home at One Sansome gives us room to scale AI impact and research, reinforcing our long-term commitment to San Francisco.

by Patrick Wendell and Matei Zaharia

  • Databricks expands AI research and opens One Sansome, our New San Francisco Headquarters.
  • The new global HQ will have 235,000 square feet, and is part of our $1 billion+ commitment to SF.
  • San Francisco is home to Databricks AI research and product teams that are building for customers pushing the boundaries of what data and AI can do, like Anthropic, Cognition, Cursor, Decagon, and OpenAI.

Last week, we opened our new headquarters at One Sansome Street in San Francisco, welcoming employees, customers, and partners into what will ultimately be a 235,000+ square foot space that matches the scale of what we're building together.

Data is increasingly becoming the engine that powers frontier AI, and this investment lets us better serve customers like Anthropic, Cognition, Cursor, Decagon, and OpenAI. The move is only part of our long-term commitment to San Francisco as our home base for building the future of data and AI for the world’s most innovative organizations. The Bay Area's concentration of top universities, research institutions, and technical talent is unmatched.

As previously shared, we're investing over $1 billion into our San Francisco operations by early 2028. We've committed to hosting our Data + AI Summit here through 2030, which is expected to generate nearly $1 billion in economic value for the city. This year’s event drew over 30,000 attendees, a record that we plan to beat in 2027.

San Francisco is the central hub for our AI Research team, which is innovating on the frontier of AI agents and models for knowledge work to power products like Genie, including:

  • KARL: custom models for enterprise that do better than frontier models on all three dimensions: inference cost, latency, and quality.
  • MemCurrent: a persistent memory architecture for production agents that keeps important, relevant information consistent and fresh for faster, more efficient responses. With MemCurrent, which powers Genie and Agent Bricks Memory, AI agents aren’t starting from zero every time.
  • Adaptive Instructed Retriever: a more efficient way for AI agents to find the right tables, notebooks, dashboards, and documents for better, faster results. Instead of brute-force exploration, agents adjust their search strategy based on the request. Sequential search is reserved for only the more complex, multi-step prompts.

Additionally, the teams at One Sansome are building some of Databricks’ most important products that drive real-world impact, such as:

  • Lakebase: the first serverless Postgres database built for AI agents.
  • Genie: An always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work.
  • Unity Gateway: multi-AI governance and cost controls.

When we initially announced this lease in March last year, we shared that the space would have over 150,000 square feet. Last week, we opened our doors with 201,000 square feet, and by next fall will expand to 235,000 square feet. Our new One Sansome headquarters offers significantly more room to collaborate, and there are tons of new benefits and amenities for Databricks employees, customers, and partners, including:

  • Modern collaboration spaces: Conference rooms with best-in-class acoustics.
  • Dining and recreation: a game room, a larger café, a coffee bar, and more.
  • Video and podcast studios: a video studio, podcast recording space, and green room.
  • Executive Briefing Center: a dedicated space for customer and partner meetings, featuring modern conference facilities and comfortable lounge areas.
  • Fitness facilities: a fitness center with locker rooms, showers, and towel service.
  • Transit and neighborhood: direct MUNI and BART access from the Montgomery Street station, and just steps from Yerba Buena, Powell Street, and Chinatown.

For us, this move is also a chance to reflect on how far we’ve come and what comes next. In 2015, we went from a small office in downtown Berkeley to 160 Spear Street in San Francisco. We had fewer than 100 employees. At the time, the new space felt enormous, and it was a huge validation that we were onto something real.

A lot has happened since then. We've grown from a scrappy open-source startup to a leader in data and AI, now with over 12,000 employees worldwide. In August, we announced crossing a $7 billion revenue run-rate, with >80% YoY growth and closed funding at a $190B valuation.

Over the last decade, we have grown to help 20,000+ customers, like adidas, AT&T, Bayer, Block, Mastercard, Rivian, Unilever, and 70% of the Fortune 500. We’ve welcomed powerhouse teams from acquisitions like Mosaic, Neon, Tabular, Row Zero, and Panther, many of which are Bay Area companies that chose to join forces with us. We’ve developed and released market-leading products like Lakebase, Genie, and Unity Gateway.

Spear Street was home to all of that growth, but we knew it was time for a change. In March 2025, we announced plans to move to One Sansome: a new headquarters that could keep pace with our momentum and our ambitions. Now, we're thrilled to be here.

We’re excited for our employees, customers, and partners to experience our new office at One Sansome. If you’re interested in building the future of data and AI, check out our careers page!

entries.content:
Genie is always on, proactively working alongside you on long-running enterprise tasks, grounded in your business context, within your organization’s guardrails.

by Cynthya Peranandam and Elise Georis

• Genie is now an autonomous AI coworker that handles long-running tasks on your behalf, operating within the guardrails you set.

• Genie Ontology, an agentic ontology built by agents and governed by people, provides trusted business context, while Genie Search finds information across your lakehouse and business systems to help Genie deliver accurate and complete answers.

• Unity Gateway lets admins control tool access, trace actions, and set spending limits to keep autonomy under control.

AI assistants can run analyses and summarize meetings, but employees still manage the work around them. That’s because most enterprise work is continuous, complex, and data-intensive. To monitor pipeline performance or manage budgets, someone has to track changes, decide what matters, and take action.

Earlier this year, we introduced Genie One to help teams understand their data and act on it. Thousands of customers use Genie in production, including Zillow, Unilever, adidas, Atlassian, and AstraZeneca.

Today, we’re introducing the new Genie: an autonomous AI coworker that proactively handles long-running enterprise work for you. Genie stays on the job continuously, tracking progress, following up on missing inputs, and taking action as new information arrives. You set the guardrails, supervise its work, and approve where needed, and Genie takes care of the rest.

That autonomy depends on business context and clear controls. Genie Ontology gives Genie a map of your business, including its definitions, metrics, relationships, and organizational knowledge. Genie Search helps people and agents find information across your lakehouse and connected business applications. Unity Gateway and Unity Catalog govern Genie within your existing permissions and policies, while giving admins visibility into its actions, usage, and cost.

You can work with Genie through Genie One, email, Slack, and Microsoft Teams. Give it a job and access to the tools it needs, and it takes responsibility for ongoing work. It checks in when it needs input or approval, and it adapts to your feedback.

For example, Genie can monitor incoming insurance claims for emerging fraud patterns and loss-ratio drift, then assemble the case file and route it to underwriters when a segment moves outside guidelines. In marketing, Genie can manage campaigns around the clock, investigate any underperformance, and propose weekly budget changes for approval. It can also monitor your email and Slack, prepare you for the day, and alert you as new things come up.

What makes this possible is context from Genie Ontology, which tells Genie how your business works—from what counts as an active customer to which revenue metric is authoritative. Personal memory retains your preferences and instructions, so you don’t have to repeat them for every job.

Genie is also proactive. It notices work you repeat, like a weekly update, and offers to take it on. It can also flag issues that need your attention even before you set up a job. Once a job is running, it can run on a schedule or respond to triggers, such as when a metric dips or when more than 10 customers ask for the same feature.

Genie can work on many jobs at once. You can supervise, steer, and stop them in one conversation, with a control panel for active jobs and outputs. You decide what Genie does on its own and what needs your sign-off, within your company guardrails.

We're also expanding Genie with new ways to find information, create finished work, and collaborate across tools.

One place to find answers: Search employees, documents, tickets, and more from the same chat bar where you ask questions. Genie Search brings results from sources like Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, Confluence, and Workday together with Databricks dashboards, tables, Databricks Apps, and Genie Agents. Organizational directories help you explore team structures and find the right colleague.

Artifacts ready to share: Describe the slide deck, dashboard, or interactive HTML page you need, and Genie builds it directly in the conversation. Refine it in chat, then present, share, or reuse it. Scheduled tasks keep each artifact current as your data changes, while shared skills apply company brand guidelines.

"With artifacts in Genie, we have full creative control over how we present our data. We can get the exact look and feel we want while keeping everything connected to our governed data — it's the best of both worlds."- Guilherme Vivian, Data Manager, Agibank

Work across applications: MCP connectors let Genie read from and take action in popular tools like Slack, Zoom, Microsoft 365, Jira, GitHub, and your calendar, all grounded in the same ontology that gives Genie the definitions, relationships, and context to understand your business. Through custom MCP you can also connect to ServiceNow, PagerDuty and more: Genie can investigate an incident using GitHub and Jira changes, keep the ticket fresh, and keep the team updated until the issue is resolved. And when someone gets great results from a repeatable workflow, they can publish it as a skill and share it with their team. Skills live in Unity Catalog and run with the permissions of whoever uses them.

Genie wherever you work: Message or @mention Genie in Slack and Microsoft Teams, or use it in your browser, on desktop, and on iOS and Android. Plugins also bring Genie’s business context into AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude.

Genie works alongside every business user, and Genie Agents bring specialized expertise to entire teams. Thousands of teams already use them in marketing, sales, finance, and operations. A department configures an agent with the data, files, tools, and instructions it needs, then manages its access and use. Teams can work with agents in Genie One or through APIs, custom applications, and automated workflows.

Work across structured and unstructured data: Genie Agents now works across not only structured tables but also PDFs, slides, and more. Content search in Unity Catalog Volumes makes this possible without a separate vector index. A sales leader asking why a region is losing deals can get an analysis that combines pipeline data and win-loss reports, with page-level citations that make the supporting evidence easy to inspect.

From investigation to action: Connectors let Genie Agents read from and act in tools including Slack, Atlassian, GitHub, Gmail, Google Drive, and Microsoft 365. An agent can investigate an issue, create a ticket, and prepare a summary for the team's channel, carrying the findings into the systems where teams work.

Share expertise beyond your organization: OpenSharing for Genie Agents lets teams share governed agents with partners and customers, pre-loaded with the data, instructions, and knowledge they need to get value right away. For more sensitive use cases, Genie Clean Rooms lets recipients ask questions and get answers without exposing the underlying data or proprietary logic, with controls such as conversation and output limits.

"Genie Agents let our domain experts productize their knowledge of the data directly. What used to take a full development cycle now takes days, and every answer stays inside our governance boundary."- Priyanka John, Vice President, S&P Global Energy

Whether Genie manages a single task or an ongoing responsibility, it needs to understand your business and how information across systems connects. Genie Ontology gives AI across your company that shared understanding. It connects structured and unstructured data with definitions, relationships, and organizational knowledge.

Built by agents, governed by people: Agents build most of Genie Ontology automatically from the dashboards, queries, and notebooks people already use, and it keeps learning with every query and AI interaction across your organization. External knowledge sources extend that learning to business logic in BI tools such as Power BI. Teams establish authoritative definitions in Unity Catalog, and the OntoRank algorithm gives those definitions precedence, so every agent works from the same governed understanding of the business.

Understand people and teams: Organizational directories, starting with Workday, bring people, teams, and reporting relationships into Genie Ontology. OntoRank combines those relationships with activity signals that show who actually works together, so Genie can weigh what's most relevant to the person asking.

Retain admin controls: Ontology Manager gives teams a shared place to manage and customize context as the business evolves. Admins can monitor context health, while domain experts curate the knowledge they know best. Unity Catalog Domains, Pages, and Ontology Snippets support both expert-curated definitions and the knowledge Genie learns automatically. Proactive gap alerts flag frequently asked-about concepts that lack governed definitions, and owners can promote useful learned knowledge into authoritative Pages.

Shared business context also helps improve accuracy and reduce token use. In a new benchmark built with Turing, we compared Genie, powered by Genie Ontology, with two leading frontier agents on the same tasks in the same Databricks workspace. Genie answered correctly in 91% of task runs, 1.6 times the rate of the stronger frontier agent, while using less than half as many tokens. The tasks required connecting knowledge spread across tables, dashboards, and notebooks, not simply accessing data.

"Genie Ontology is exactly what we need to scale AI without losing the business context that makes it useful. It's a force multiplier for our data teams." - Noah Cepela, SVP, Analytics and Insights, Mode Global

Genie Ontology gives Genie a shared understanding of your business. To put that understanding to work, Genie also needs to find relevant information wherever it lives, from lakehouse tables to documents, tickets, and wikis. Just as importantly, it needs to enforce each asset’s access controls.

Today, we're introducing Genie Search, a new kind of hybrid AI search that brings enterprise search into Databricks, with no separate search infrastructure to procure and no separate permission model to maintain.

Genie Search combines an index of content from core business apps like Google Drive, Jira, Confluence, Workday, and SharePoint with live search through MCP. The index provides fast, accurate access, while MCP retrieves the most recent updates and the long tail of apps that can't be indexed. For each task, Genie draws from the index, MCP, or SQL, then composes one answer with citations. The result is more complete answers with fewer tool calls and tokens.

Beyond the standard benefits of a search index, Genie Search also feeds Genie Ontology, so your tickets and documents become evidence OntoRank weighs when deciding which sources to trust. Through Unity Catalog, Genie Search maps each source's access controls alongside its content and enforces them before returning any results, so nobody sees a document in Genie that they couldn't open in the original application.

The same business context that powers Genie can also support work in other AI assistants. Connect your data once, let Genie build your ontology from how your teams work, then bring that context through Genie plugins to ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and Grok Bot. You can also use Genie MCP directly to connect Genie to other AI tools.

Agents can hand an entire business question to Genie or request the context needed for a larger task. Genie applies governed definitions, respects user permissions, and cites its sources.

As Genie takes on ongoing work across enterprise systems, admins need to control who uses it, what it can access, and how much it costs. Unity Gateway brings those controls together, letting admins govern Genie alongside coding agents, models, MCP tools, and skills.

Data access: Genie acts with your identity and accesses only information you’re authorized to see. It respects Unity Catalog permissions and, for content indexed by Genie Search, each source system’s permissions. When users need additional access, Genie can prepare an access request for them to review and send. Admins and data owners retain approval authority.

Tools and actions: Admins control connector access, MCP tools, and approval requirements. Business users choose what Genie can do autonomously within those limits. Unity Catalog governs reusable skills, and the same controls apply when external agents such as Claude call Genie through MCP.

Usage, cost, and auditing: Every action Genie takes is traced and auditable. Admins can set workspace and per-user budgets, spending caps, and alerts. They can also ask Genie to investigate usage and agent traces for wasted tokens and costly tool calls.

With Genie, teams can move from asking AI for help with individual tasks to giving it responsibility for ongoing work, with shared business context and controls built in. Learn more:

  • Genie: New announcements  |  Product overview
  • Genie Ontology & Genie Search: New announcements  |  Product overview
  • Genie Agents: New announcements  |  Product overview
  • Genie plugins: New announcements

entries.title: Genie with Genie Ontology Delivers 1.6× the Accuracy with Less than Half the Tokens
entries.summary: We developed a new enterprise data-agent benchmark in collaboration with Turing to...
entries.content:
An enterprise benchmark developed with Turing compares Genie using Genie Ontology with two leading frontier agents.

by Jeff Fletcher and Rishabh Singh

  • A new, shareable benchmark built with Turing compares Genie with two frontier agents on business questions in a live Databricks workspace.
  • Genie passed 91% of runs, compared with 45% and 58% for the frontier agents, while using less than half the tokens and finishing three to four times faster.
  • Genie’s superior performance is attributable to the business context present in notebooks, dashboards and saved SQL queries extracted by Genie Ontology.

We developed a new enterprise data-agent benchmark in collaboration with Turing to compare Genie with two major frontier agents and their respective harnesses on business questions in a live Databricks workspace. The evaluation measures answer accuracy, token usage and time to complete the task. Genie had a 91% pass rate, compared with 45% and 58% for the other frontier agents, while using fewer than half the tokens.

Unlike previous data agent benchmarks that typically only include tables, this benchmark also includes notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries, documents, and other analytical assets that capture enterprise knowledge, business definitions, and calculation rules. These assets provide key enterprise context that table schemas alone cannot establish. Genie Ontology is the enterprise context layer that gives every AI agent a shared understanding of the business. It automatically extracts and organizes this knowledge, surfacing relevant context for Genie to use when answering questions.

Our previous evaluation of Genie with ontology used a proprietary dataset. This benchmark evaluates Genie using tasks and supporting analytical assets designed for sharing, so others can also run the evaluation.

Answering business questions correctly requires accessing the institutional knowledge about how an organization interprets and uses its data. Teams develop this knowledge through everyday analytical work: establishing revenue definitions, maintaining dashboards that reflect current reporting rules, and writing queries that handle business-specific exceptions. The questions in this benchmark require agents to access and reason about this knowledge to perform the tasks correctly.

There are already many existing data agent benchmarks, but none that truly emulate real-world usage. We needed a benchmark that tested agents' ability to discover and use business knowledge distributed across notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries and other documents.

Existing data agent benchmarks mostly focus on a set of tables and the pipeline code that builds them, and the performance on these benchmarks is similar between the agents. In real-world enterprise tasks, it’s seldom the case that the correct answer comes from the tables alone. It requires leveraging information from many different sources, such as a specific notebook that builds the reporting tables, the SQL behind a team's dashboard, or saved queries. The questions in this benchmark require the agent to reason about the knowledge residing in these assets and combine them to correctly answer the questions.

For this benchmark, we developed a fictional company called Calderwick Energy, a UK electricity and gas supplier, whose challenges closely resemble those of many typical data teams. There are hundreds of tables (the largest has around 120 million rows of half-hourly meter data), along with assets that different teams have built on top of them, such as notebooks, scheduled jobs, dashboards, saved SQL queries, code, metrics, documents, and Genie Agents. It also has the messiness of a real-world scenario, like copied notebooks, abandoned analyses, old documents and dev copies, frozen reporting tables and dashboards nobody has touched in months.

We created multiple data analytics questions and as queries as the benchmark tasks and ran each agent 5 times per task against the same live Databricks workspace.

We compare the agents on three primary metrics:

  • Accuracy (the percentage of responses that satisfy the task’s grading criteria)
  • Token usage (the average number of tokens used per run)
  • Wall time (the average amount of time taken per run)

The Table below shows the overall performance of the three agents on this benchmark. Genie solves 91% of the tasks correctly, compared to 45% for frontier Agent A and 58% for frontier Agent B. Moreover, Genie is significantly faster (4x compared to Agent A and 3x compared to Agent B) and much more token-efficient, as it can leverage the Genie Ontology to identify and reason about relevant enterprise context more efficiently.

Agent Pass Rate Avg wall time (per run) Avg tokens (per run)
Genie 91.0% 100.3 431,829
Agent A 45.0% 434.6 889,019
Agent B 58.0% 306.5 1,051,070

You can read more about how Genie Ontology works in the GA announcement blog or in the official documentation.

If you want to replicate this benchmark on your own workspace, reach out to your account team, and they can help you set it up to help implement this and show how well Genie works on a live Databricks workspace.

In addition to Genie, we evaluated two leading coding/knowledge agents, “Agent A” and “Agent B,” from frontier AI labs in our results. Genie ran natively, while the other agents connected through a Databricks toolbelt. They all received the same question. The toolbelt specifically excluded the Genie MCP because it would give those other agents access to all the Genie capabilities we were testing.

We checked whether each agent answered correctly using a calibrated grading rubric that captures the desired answers and agent behaviors. Where small differences in the numbers were acceptable, we set those limits in advance. An answer passed only if it met the required checks in the grading rubric. We also recorded how the agents found and used the business context needed to answer the question. The traces show which snippets Genie retrieved and the queries the agents chose to run. In addition to accuracy, we also measure latency and token usage for each agent.

From the results, we observe that Genie’s correct answer pass rate is significantly better than both frontier agents, Agent A (+46%) and Agent B (+33%). It is also significantly faster (3-4x) while using less than half the tokens on average. We now provide a qualitative analysis of how Genie efficiently answers these questions correctly.

The following is an example task in the benchmark that asks agents to identify one of Calderwick Energy’s historical Commercial planning rates:

This looks like a straightforward lookup. The bill cost stack table has a column called 

cfd_rate_p
, and the rows for FY24/25 contain 0.31 pence per kWh. An agent can find the relevant table, filter to the requested period, and return that number. Checking more rows would reinforce the answer: the same rate appears throughout the table.

The detail that changes the answer is already recorded in the notebook that builds the bill cost stack.

It explains that Commercial sets planning rates annually, and that the mart uses FY25/26 assumptions, including when those assumptions are applied to earlier billing periods. A separate section, “Planning rates by year,” preserves the history:

Fiscal year CfD planning rate
FY24/25 0.52 p/kWh
FY25/26 0.31 p/kWh
FY26/27 draft 0.45 p/kWh

The question asks which planning rate the Commercial team set for FY24/25. The rate currently applied to those rows reflects FY25/26 assumptions. The notebook already documents this distinction and preserves the historical rate needed to answer the question.

Genie Ontology surfaced a snippet containing the historical planning rates and linked it to the source notebook, 

45_mart_bill_cost_stack
. When we ran the task, Genie inspected the notebook to confirm the rate and returned 0.52 p/kWh in its first response. The Ontology panel showed both the relevant information and the notebook it came from, allowing us to check the source.

Across the 5 Genie runs, the first answer was 0.52 every time. The other agents did not get the correct historical rate across their runs. One returned 0.31 throughout. The other reported 0.31, questioned whether a year-specific planning rate was documented, or both.

Answering correctly required understanding what the rate in the table represented and finding the historical planning assumptions documented by the Commercial team. Genie Ontology made that existing knowledge available as context for Genie’s response.

The frontier agents are very good at doing most things based on written text. Type the words for a task that can be done with a computer, and an LLM will understand the requirement and then create and execute a plan to complete that task. Each new model release adds incrementally more capability, and the frontier labs seem to swap out the No. 1 spot on the various benchmark tests.

This effectively commoditizes the token-generating ‘intelligence’ and puts the source of the power and capability of the agents into the harness and the context they can retrieve. This is why this benchmark shows how much context matters and how Genie Ontology is optimized to provide the relevant context for the task at hand. For a competing agent, retrieving all the artifacts and metadata needed to extract the relevant context is time-consuming and expensive, and it does not necessarily guarantee the correct result. These benchmark results make the case for using Genie (both the UI and the MCP) and Genie Code as the most reliable and cost-effective data agent and the entry point for your AI coworker.

The benchmark is intended to test Genie and other agents operating within an established Databricks deployment, with relevant data governed by Unity Catalog and business knowledge captured in workspace assets. Agents need to discover and use the correct context. In new deployments that have not had time to accumulate workspace knowledge, or when questions can be answered directly from tables and schemas, the difference between agents may be smaller. This explains why other existing data agent benchmarks show smaller differences between agents.

To learn more, reach out to your account team to get access to this benchmark, and they can help you set it up to help showcase how Genie works on a busy Databricks workspace.
